title: Regulation and risk warnings
summary: How licences, entities, marketing permission, platform policies and influencer rules apply to trading offers, with a country-by-country map of our core African markets. You finish able to verify any broker or exchange, place warnings people actually see, and apply exact go/no-go gates per geo. Education, not legal advice.

lessons.title: How trading regulation really works
objectives: By the end you can explain the difference between a licence to operate and permission to market.
You can explain passporting, offshore entities and reverse solicitation, and why ads change the picture.
You can build an entity map for every geo you target.
You can apply a go/no-go rule to a broker's cross-border marketing.

steps.h: Why a licence is not the whole answer
steps.p: In the Operator school you learned that a broker must be licensed. Here we go one level deeper. A broker can hold a real licence and still not be allowed to market to people in your country. Your ad is the marketing, so that gap becomes your problem.

d.b: A licence to operate is not a licence to market
d.s: Your ad decides which rules apply.

steps.say: In the Operator school you learned that a broker must be licensed. Here we go one level deeper. Look at the headline: a licence to operate is not a licence to market. A broker can hold a real licence and still not be allowed to market to people in your country. And since your ad is the marketing, that gap becomes your problem. Your ad decides which rules apply.

steps.h: Four ideas behind every trading rule
steps.p: Most confusion about trading regulation comes from mixing these four ideas. Keep them separate when you ask questions, and you will get clearer answers from networks, brokers and advisers.
d: Authorisation|Permission to run the business, from a regulator
Financial promotion|Rules on who may advertise and how
Entity per geo|Which company in the group serves each country
Cross-border rules|Whether a foreign firm may approach residents
steps.say: Most confusion about trading regulation comes from mixing four ideas. Look at the cards. Authorisation, permission to run the business, from a regulator. Financial promotion, the rules on who may advertise and how. Entity per geo, which company in the group serves each country. And cross-border rules, whether a foreign firm may approach residents. Keep these separate when you ask questions, and you'll get clearer answers from networks, brokers and advisers.

steps.p: Large brokers often run one brand through several legal entities, each licensed somewhere different. Users in each country are sent to a different entity with different protections. Your ad decides which one your users meet.
steps.say: This map shows one brand, several companies. Follow the lines. The brand group owns an E U entity, a South Africa entity and an offshore entity, each licensed somewhere different. Now look at the bottom: your ad reaches a user in Kenya, and that user signs with the offshore entity. Users in each country are sent to a different entity, with different protections. Your ad decides which one your users meet.

steps.h: Example: the same brand in four countries
steps.p: Illustrative example, not a real broker. The protections a user gets, such as leverage limits, negative balance protection and complaint routes, depend on the entity, not the brand on your ad.
steps.say: Here's an illustrative example, not a real broker. The same brand in four countries. A user in the U K meets Brand U K Limited, regulated by the F C A, with the standard C F D, contract for difference, warning. In the E U, Brand E U Limited, regulated by CySEC. In South Africa, a local company regulated by the F S C A, so ask the broker about the warning. In Kenya, an offshore entity, so ask, and check local rules. Protections like leverage limits, negative balance protection and complaint routes depend on the entity, not the brand.

steps.p: These three ideas explain most cross-border questions. Rules below are a rough guide at the time of writing; they differ by country and some are changing, so confirm with the regulator or an adviser.
steps.more: Reverse solicitation is narrow where it exists. European regulators have said that firms cannot rely on it when they or their partners actively market to clients. As an affiliate, your ad is active marketing, so an offshore broker that relies on users 'finding it themselves' may not be able to rely on that for your traffic. We are not certain how each African regulator treats these situations; when the answer is unclear, treat it as a no until you have advice.
d: Passporting|An EU-licensed firm can serve other EU states after notifying. Not Africa
Offshore entity|Licensed in a small jurisdiction; may lack permission in your users' country
Reverse solicitation|Some regimes let a firm serve a client who came on their own initiative
Why ads break it|If you advertise to them, they did not come on their own
steps.say: These three ideas explain most cross-border questions. Passporting: an E U-licensed firm can serve other E U states after notifying, but not Africa. Offshore entity: licensed in a small jurisdiction, and it may lack permission in your users' country. Reverse solicitation: some regimes let a firm serve a client who came on their own initiative. And here's why ads break it: if you advertise to them, they didn't come on their own. We're not certain how each African regulator treats this, so when it's unclear, treat it as a no until you have advice.

steps.h: In many places, promoting is itself regulated
steps.p: In the UK, a financial promotion must be made or approved by an authorised firm, and breaking that rule can be a criminal offence. Other countries have their own rules on who may promote investments. An affiliate can be caught by these rules, not only the broker.
steps.more: At the time of writing, the UK's rule sits in section 21 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000. Many countries have similar ideas in their securities or consumer protection laws, though the details differ. We are not certain of the exact promotion rules in each of our core African markets; check the regulator's website and, before you scale, get local advice.

d.b: You can be the one breaking the rule
d.s: Promotion rules can apply to affiliates and influencers.

steps.say: In many places, promoting is itself regulated. In the U K, a financial promotion must be made or approved by an authorised firm, and breaking that rule can be a criminal offence. Other countries have their own rules on who may promote investments. Look at the headline: you can be the one breaking the rule. Promotion rules can apply to affiliates and influencers, not only the broker. We're not certain of the exact rules in each of our core African markets, so check the regulator's website and get local advice before you scale.

steps.h: Worked example: the cost of the wrong entity
steps.p: Example. You send 40 qualified FTDs at $65 each from a geo where the broker's entity turns out not to be permitted. The network withholds the payout for a non-permitted geo. Instead of a $600 profit, you are down $2,000 of spend.
steps.more: Example maths: 40 × $65 = $2,600 expected. $2,600 − $2,000 = $600 profit if paid. If withheld, the result is −$2,000. The figures are illustrative and many networks would not behave this way, but most terms give them the right to refuse payment for traffic that breaks rules. Users also lose: they may have signed with an entity that gives them fewer protections than they assumed.
d: $2,000 spend
$600 at risk
steps.say: Here's an example of the cost of the wrong entity. You send forty qualified F T Ds, first time deposits, at sixty five dollars each, so two thousand six hundred dollars expected. Your spend was two thousand dollars, so that's six hundred dollars profit if paid. But the broker's entity turns out not to be permitted in that geo, and the network withholds the payout. Instead of six hundred dollars profit, you're down two thousand dollars. The figures are illustrative, but most terms let networks refuse payment for traffic that breaks rules. And users lose protections too.

steps.h: Why a network listing is not proof
steps.p: Networks list offers; they do not guarantee them. Clone firms copy real brokers' names and licence numbers, and unlicensed firms can pay affiliates well for months before users find they cannot withdraw. Ten minutes on a register protects your users, your account and your payouts.

d.s: A listing, a logo or a licence number on a website proves nothing.

steps.say: Networks list offers, they don't guarantee them. Look at the headline: verify it yourself, every time. A listing, a logo, or a licence number on a website proves nothing. Ten minutes on a register protects your users, your account and your payouts.

steps.say: Registers show more than a yes or no. These screens are illustrative mock-ups. Tap Next to follow each step. First, search the legal name, using the entity name from the client agreement, not the brand on the ad. Second, read the status. Look for authorised or licensed. Suspended, revoked, or no longer authorised means stop. Third, read the permissions, and check the firm may deal in your product, for example C F Ds, contracts for difference, and with retail clients. Fourth, match the websites and contacts on the register with the offer's landing page.

steps.p: Wording differs by regulator, but these are the common meanings. If you are unsure what a status means, read the regulator's help page or ask them; most publish a short guide.
d: Authorised or licensed|May carry out the listed activities
Suspended|Temporarily not allowed. Stop
Revoked or no longer authorised|Licence ended. Stop
Registered for AML only|Not the same as a full licence
Tied agent or appointed representative|Acts under another firm's licence
Not found|Treat as unlicensed until proven
steps.say: Here's what register statuses usually mean. Wording differs by regulator. Authorised or licensed, may carry out the listed activities. Suspended, temporarily not allowed, so stop. Revoked or no longer authorised, the licence ended, so stop. Registered for A M L, anti-money-laundering, only, which is not the same as a full licence. Tied agent or appointed representative, acting under another firm's licence. And not found, treat it as unlicensed until proven. If unsure, read the regulator's help page or ask them.

steps.h: Warning lists and where to look
steps.p: Regulators publish lists of firms they believe are unlicensed or are clones. Search the brand name, the legal name and the domain. Lists are not complete, so a clean search is a pass, not a guarantee.

CySEC warnings|Cyprus regulator's investor alerts
IOSCO I-SCAN|Searches warnings from many regulators at once
Local regulators|SEC Nigeria, CMA Kenya, FSCA, SEC Ghana alerts
Court and news|Search the name plus 'withdrawal' or 'scam'
steps.say: Regulators publish lists of firms they believe are unlicensed or clones. Look at the cards. The F C A Warning List, the U K regulator's list. CySEC warnings, the Cyprus regulator's investor alerts. IOSCO I-SCAN, which searches warnings from many regulators at once. Local regulators, like S E C Nigeria, C M A Kenya, the F S C A, and S E C Ghana alerts. And court and news, searching the name plus withdrawal or scam. Search the brand, legal name and domain. Lists aren't complete, so a clean search is a pass, not a guarantee.

steps.h: Clone firm versus the real firm
steps.p: A clone uses a real firm's name and licence number but its own website and contact details. The giveaway is almost always a mismatch between what the register shows and what the offer page shows.

a.title: Clone signs
items: Domain not listed on the register
Gmail or messaging-app contact only
Phone and address differ from register
Very new website for an old firm

b.title: Real firm signs
items: Domain listed or confirmed by the firm
Company email on the listed domain
Contacts match the register
Consistent history

steps.say: A clone uses a real firm's name and licence number, but its own website and contacts. On the left, clone signs: a domain not listed on the register, a Gmail or messaging-app contact only, a phone and address that differ from the register, and a very new website for an old firm. On the right, real firm signs: a domain listed or confirmed by the firm, company email on that domain, contacts that match, and a consistent history. The giveaway is almost always a mismatch between the register and the offer page.

steps.p: Crypto firms are regulated differently in each country, and many regimes are new. The checks below are a starting list at the time of writing; confirm the current rules for your geo.

steps.h: Why a hidden warning does not count
steps.p: Regulators often judge whether a warning is prominent, not only whether it exists. A warning in grey text below the fold, or cut off on mobile, can fail a review even if it is technically present. A warning people see also brings you users who understand the risk.
